thread.title: Brexit plan clears first hurdle but tough part lies ahead

author: William Watts
title: Brexit plan clears first hurdle but tough part lies ahead
text:
British Prime Minister Theresa May won a hard-fought victory Wednesday as her cabinet approved a draft plan for exiting the European Union, but bigger battles —and the potential for more market volatility—lie ahead.
After a five-hour meeting, a majority of May’s cabinet signed off on the controversial draft exit plan. But news reports said the cabinet was split, with several ministers opposed to the agreement.
NEW: told cabinet very split. May got it through on majority. Told that nearly 10 cabinet ministers opposed. Mood worse than after Chequers then? “Yeah, much much worse”
— Beth Rigby (@BethRigby) November 14, 2018 British stocks UKX, -0.28% ended lower ahead of May’s statement on Wednesday, while the British pound GBPUSD, +0.0693% saw choppy trade versus the dollar over the course of the day before rallying in the wake of the statement to trade at $1.3032, a gain of 0.4%.
U.S. stocks appeared to trim losses after May said she won cabinet approval, but ended the day in negative territory , with the S&P 500 SPX, -0.76% down 0.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, -0.81% posting a loss of more than 200 points, or 0.8%, dragged in the red by losses from component Apple Inc. AAPL, -2.82%
The U.K. is due to leave the EU in March. Failure to secure an agreement would result in a hard Brexit. That means no deal in place to govern the U.K.’s relationship with the bloc. The tentative plan agreed to by the cabinet would end the free movement of labor, a key goal of Brexit supporters, but see the U.K. remain in a customs union with the EU until London and Brussels reach a trade agreement. Such an arrangement would eliminate the need for a hard border between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.
Some critics, including hard-line Brexit lawmakers within May’s own Conservative Party, charge that the deal fails to adequately deliver on Brexit. And with the Conservatives lacking a majority in the House of Commons, May’s government relies on the support of Northern Ireland’s Democratic Unionist Party, which described the text of the Brexit agreement as a “poor deal,” according to the BBC .
Meanwhile, hard-line pro-Brexit Conservative members of parliament attacked the deal. One of the leading pro-Brexit lawmakers, Jacob Rees-Mogg, called the draft a “rubbish deal.”
May could face a leadership challenges. Otherwise, a deal would still need to be approved by the remaining 27 EU member states. An emergency summit of EU leaders is expected later this month.
The most difficult aspect will likely remain the parliamentary vote on a Brexit deal, but opposition to the plan from both pro- and anti-Brexit politicians as well as the misgivings of the DUP sets the stage for “significant political upheaval” in coming weeks, said Andrew Goodwin, economist at Oxford Economics, in a note.
Opposition by euroskeptic Conservatives could leave May to rely on votes by opposition Labour members of parliament, who would have to defy their own leaders to back the deal.
“Unless there is a dramatic shift among Tory and Labour MPs, it looks very difficult for May to win the critical vote,” wrote Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group. “On our figures, if 15 Labour MPs back her deal and 30 Tories oppose it, she would lose by 328 votes to 311 votes if she has DUP support and lose by 338 votes to 301 votes if the DUP opposes the deal.”
The bottom line is that the potential for further volatility in financial markets, Goodwin said.
“There is a good chance that it will take more than one attempt—and for it to be made clear that this is a ‘take it or leave it’ choice—to secure a parliamentary majority,” he said. “And a ‘no-deal’ scenario remains a very live risk.”
